Literature Verification: Almost-Sure Morse–Smale
Property (No Saddle Connections) for Stationary
Gaussian Fields on the 2-Torus
TL;DR
No existing published result proves the almost-sure no-saddle-connection (global
Morse–Smale) statement for Gaussian fields. The literature reliably stops at “almost
surely Morse” (nondegenerate critical points) and “almost surely distinct critical values”;
the transversality of stable/unstable manifolds — the global Morse–Smale condition — is
genuinely open/folklore for every random-field ensemble checked. Your earlier sweep is
confirmed.
The strongest existing building blocks for the parametric-transversality route,
ranked, are: (i) the Peccati–Stecconi Cameron–Martin/Malliavin “ray absolute continuity”
framework for Gaussian-field functionals; (ii) the classical Abraham–Robbin parametric
transversality theorem; and (iii) the deterministic Smale/Kupka–Smale/Peixoto genericity
theory into which the probabilistic argument must be parametrized. Bulinskaya-type
lemmas (Azaïs–Wschebor Prop. 6.12; Adler–Taylor Lemma 11.2.10) discharge the
auxiliary Morse and distinct-critical-value degeneracies but do NOT reach saddle
connections.
The key obstruction is real and must be handled explicitly: symmetric/degenerate-spectrum fields can force saddle connections (the vertical torus of revolution is the
canonical deterministic example), so any theorem must exclude degenerate spectra and
cannot rely on any finite jet — a saddle-saddle connection is a global gradient-flow
constraint, not an equal-height coincidence detectable by naive Kac–Rice.
Key Findings
1. No a.s. Morse–Smale result exists for random fields. Across Gaussian fields, random
trigonometric polynomials, random spherical harmonics, Kostlan polynomials, and
Riemannian random waves, no paper proves or even states as a theorem the transversality
of stable/unstable manifolds (equivalently, absence of saddle-saddle gradient connections).
The community consistently proves only the local Morse condition. This is the central
verdict.

2. “Almost surely Morse” and “almost surely distinct critical values” ARE established,
with exact hypotheses, chiefly by Beliaev–McAuley–Muirhead and, in the manifold setting,
via Azaïs–Wschebor / Adler–Taylor Bulinskaya lemmas. These fold directly into your file.
3. The deterministic 2D reduction you rely on is correct and citable. For 2D gradient
flows, Morse + no saddle connections ⟺ Morse–Smale, because the invariant manifolds of
index-1 saddles are 1-dimensional and transversality of two 1-manifolds in a 2-manifold is
exactly non-coincidence. This is Smale (1961) + Peixoto, packaged in Palis–de Melo and
Banyaga–Hurtubise.
4. Parametric transversality and Cameron–Martin machinery both exist, but have never
been combined and applied to gradient-flow transversality of a Gaussian ensemble. This is
precisely the gap your route (a) would fill.
Details
Item 1 — Beliaev, McAuley, Muirhead (BMM): exact conditions
Paper: “On the number of excursion sets of planar Gaussian fields.” D. Beliaev, M.
McAuley, S. Muirhead. Probability Theory and Related Fields 178 (2020), 655–698
(MR4168385, DOI 10.1007/s00440-020-00984-9); arXiv:1807.10209.
Their standing hypotheses are Conditions 1.1 on a centered, unit-variance stationary planar
Gaussian field f with spectral measure ρ:
(1) For some ν>0, f ∈ C^{2+ν}_loc(ℝ²) almost surely — holds if the covariance κ is
C^{4+ε}, equivalently ∫|λ|^{4+ε} dρ(λ) < ∞. arxiv
(2) ∇²f(0) is a non-degenerate Gaussian vector — equivalent to the support of ρ not
being contained in the union of two lines through the origin. arxiv
(3) For any t, if f(t)−f(0) is non-degenerate then (f(t)−f(0), ∇f(t), ∇f(0)) is non-degenerate — “holds provided the support of ρ is not too degenerate; in particular it
holds if the support of ρ contains an open set.” arxiv
Condition (2) is their a.s. Morse condition; conditions (2)–(3) together give the non-degeneracies needed for Kac–Rice. In the companion paper “Smoothness and
monotonicity of the excursion set density of planar Gaussian fields” (D. Beliaev, M.
McAuley, S. Muirhead, Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020), Paper No. 93, MR4136473;
arXiv:1905.09759), Lemma A.1 makes the spectral characterization explicit: “the spectral
measure µ being supported on the union of two lines through the origin is equivalent to the
Gaussian vector ∇²f(0) being degenerate,” arxiv and “if the support of µ contains an open
set then, for any distinct t₁,…,tₙ, the vector (f(tᵢ), ∇f(tᵢ), ∇²f(tᵢ)) is non-degenerate.” arxiv

Distinct critical values / aperiodicity (Item 8): In arXiv:1807.10209 they define f periodic
if there exists x≠0 with κ(x)=1, aperiodic otherwise. Verbatim (their Lemma 2.4): “A
Gaussian field which is aperiodic almost surely has no two critical points at the same level
(see Lemma 2.4), and we will show that for such fields, all saddle points of f satisfy exactly
one of the two conditions in Definition 1.7.” This is their sharpest a.s.-distinct-critical-values
statement — but note the important structural caveat below on periodicity of torus fields.
On gradient flow / separatrices / Morse–Smale: BMM use Morse theory to relate
excursion/level-set component counts to critical-point densities, and they classify saddles
as “upper connected” / “lower connected” (Definition 1.7), which is a statement about which
excursion component a saddle borders. arxiv They never address gradient-flow lines,
separatrices, stable/unstable manifolds, or the Morse–Smale (no-saddle-connection)
property. Their later works (Fluctuations, Prob. Math. Phys. 3 (2022) 105–144,
arXiv:1908.10708; CLT, Ann. Probab. 52 (2024) 882–922, arXiv:2205.09085; covariance
formula, Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré 61 (2025) 713–745, arXiv:2303.07823) continue on
component counts, not gradient structure. Classification: adaptable (hypotheses) / not-a-match (Morse–Smale content).
Item 2 — Any a.s. Morse–Smale result for random functions
Verdict: none found.
Nicolaescu (“Random Morse functions and spectral geometry,” arXiv:1209.0639;
“Critical points of multidimensional random Fourier series: central limits,” Bernoulli 24
(2018) 1128–1170; Project Euclid “An Invitation to Morse Theory”) proves random
Gaussian superpositions of Laplace eigenfunctions are a.s. Morse and studies critical-value/critical-point statistics; he does not prove a.s. Morse–Smale.
Gayet–Welschinger (e.g. “Betti numbers of random real hypersurfaces and
determinants of random symmetric matrices,” JEMS 18 (2016) 733–772; “Expected
topology of random real algebraic submanifolds,” J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 14 (2015) 673–
702) use a fixed Morse function restricted to random hypersurfaces and equidistribution
of its critical points; no gradient-flow transversality.
Sarnak–Wigman (“Topologies of nodal sets of random band-limited functions,” Comm.
Pure Appl. Math. 72 (2019) 275–342; arXiv:1312.7858/1510.08500) establish universal
laws for nodal topologies via stability/Morse-theoretic arguments, but nothing on saddle
connections.
Applied cosmology literature (Feldbrugge–van Engelen–van de Weygaert–Pranav–
Vegter, “Stochastic Homology of Gaussian vs. non-Gaussian Random Fields,” JCAP
09(2019)052; arXiv:1908.01619) computes the Morse–Smale complex of Gaussian fields
on the torus numerically. It asserts the needed regularity as automatic — verbatim: “f

should be a Morse function… and no two critical points have the same function value.
Gaussian random fields always obey these conditions” — i.e., it tacitly assumes only the
Morse + distinct-value conditions and treats the complex as well-defined, without any
rigorous a.s. transversality statement. The companion Pranav work (arXiv:2109.08721)
states the definition — “collections of ascending and descending manifolds that share
common origin and destination… If additionally, the ascending and the descending
manifolds intersect only transversally, the given function is a Morse-Smale function” —
but proves nothing about it holding a.s.
Classification: merely inspirational. The gap is real.
Item 3 — Parametric transversality for Gaussian measures
Abraham–Robbin, Transversal Mappings and Flows (Benjamin, 1967): contains the
parametric transversality theorem (Transversal Density Theorem) and the Sard-type
infinite-dimensional apparatus. Standard modern statement: if F: E×X→Y is C^s, W⊂Y a
submanifold with F ⋔ W, X finite-dimensional / W finite-codimensional and E, X second
countable, then F_e ⋔ W arxiv for a residual (and, in the finite-dimensional parameter
case, full-measure) set of e∈E. This is the deterministic engine of route (a). (Compare
the Sard–Smale/Abraham Fredholm formulation for Banach manifolds when the
parameter space is infinite-dimensional.)
Cameron–Martin / Malliavin framework (Peccati–Stecconi). “Nodal Volumes as
Differentiable Functionals of Gaussian fields,” G. Peccati and M. Stecconi, Transactions
of the AMS 378 (2025), no. 9, 6585–6654 (DOI 10.1090/tran/9440); Centre-mersenne
arXiv:2403.20243. This paper builds exactly the machinery route (a) needs: it places
geometric functionals of Gaussian fields in the Malliavin–Sobolev spaces �^{1,p} via ray
absolute continuity (their Definition 3.6, following Bogachev, Gaussian Measures, Defs.
5.2.3–5.2.4) — a functional Ψ is “ray absolutely continuous, meaning that, for every
element h of the Cameron–Martin space of X, the mapping t↦Ψ(X+th) admits an
absolutely continuous modification.” arxiv The paper explicitly “extend[s] and
generalize[s] the seminal contribution by Angst and Poly (2020)” and covers “two-dimensional manifolds, possibly with boundary and corners.” Their Theorem 1.3 gives,
for a centered C² Gaussian field on a C² compact Riemannian manifold with (X(p),
d_pX(v)) admitting a density, that the nodal set is a.s. a neat C² hypersurface and the
nodal volume is Malliavin-differentiable. arxiv Caveat: the paper concerns nodal
volumes (zero sets of the field), NOT gradient-flow / stable–unstable-manifold
transversality. The Cameron–Martin/shift structure is present and is the most plausible
existing toolkit, but it has not been applied to your problem. Related: M. Stecconi, “Kac–
Rice formula for transverse intersections,” Anal. Math. Phys. 12 (2022) no. 2, Paper 44
Springer (arXiv:2103.10853); Lerario–Stecconi, “Differential topology of Gaussian
random fields,” arXiv:1902.03805 — both develop transverse-intersection Kac–Rice

machinery (expectations), not a.s. gradient-flow transversality.
Classification: adaptable (this is the core of route (a), but requires genuinely new
work).
Item 4 — Bulinskaya’s lemma: exact statements
Both citation numbers you have are correct but refer to different books:
Azaïs & Wschebor, Level Sets and Extrema of Random Processes and Fields (Wiley,
2009): the generalized Bulinskaya lemma is Proposition 6.12 (Chapter 6, Rice
formulas). Sufficient condition: the joint density of (F(x), ∇F(x)) is bounded near (0,0)
uniformly in x over the compact domain ⟹ a.s. no degenerate zeros (0 is a.s. a regular
value). Springer Standard statement requires C¹ paths (C² if excluding degenerate
critical points, via the field (∇f, det ∇²f)). (A few papers cite adjacent numbers — “6.11”
or “6.5” — but Proposition 6.12 is the dominant, best-supported citation, per Wigman’s
survey “On the nodal structures of random fields: a decade of results,” J. Appl. Comput.
Topol.)
Adler & Taylor, Random Fields and Geometry (Springer, 2007): the analogous
statement is Lemma 11.2.10 (Chapter 11, Kac–Rice metatheorem, companion to
Theorem 11.2.1). Same essential content: (∇f, f) density bounded near (0, ℓ) uniformly
over t ⟹ a.s. no zeros of the auxiliary field. arxiv
Strengthened / codimension-two version (exactly what you need for Morse + distinct
values): apply the lemma to auxiliary fields. To exclude degenerate critical points, apply it to
(∇f, det ∇²f): ℝ² → ℝ^{d+1} (an a.s. C¹ field with bounded pointwise density), which a.s. does
not vanish — this is exactly the argument Rivera–Vanneuville and others run (“Talagrand’s
inequality in planar Gaussian field percolation,” arXiv:1905.13317, proof of Lemma 2.10,
citing “Lemma 11.2.10 of Adler–Taylor”). To exclude two critical points at equal height, apply
the same lemma to (x,y) ↦ ((f(x)−f(y))², |∇_x f|², |∇_y f|²) on a compact exhaustion of the off-diagonal �×�∖Δ. Both are codimension-counting arguments and both are within reach
of the standard Bulinskaya machinery.
Crucial limitation for your problem: these arguments detect equal-height coincidences
and finite-jet degeneracies. A saddle-saddle connection does NOT require equal critical
values (the descending separatrix of a higher saddle can reach a lower saddle), so it is
invisible to any Bulinskaya/Kac–Rice argument on a finite jet. This is the precise reason the
problem is hard and why route (a) or (b) — a genuinely global argument — is needed.
Item 5 — Deterministic Morse–Smale genericity to be parametrized
Smale, “On gradient dynamical systems,” Ann. of Math. 74 (1961) 199–206: every
Morse gradient flow can be C¹-approximated by a Morse–Smale one; a Morse flow with

no saddle-to-saddle separatrix is Morse–Smale. arxiv arxiv
Kupka–Smale theorem: Morse–Smale gradient vector fields are open and dense
among gradient vector fields on a compact manifold. Springer ResearchGate In the
gradient case, the Kupka–Smale property is equivalent to the Morse–Smale
property (genericity of Morse–Smale for gradient fields is due to Smale). arxiv Citable
form: Banyaga–Hurtubise, Lectures on Morse Homology, Theorem 6.6 (Kupka–Smale)
with the λ-Lemma (Theorem 6.17); Palis–de Melo, Geometric Theory of Dynamical
Systems; Pajitnov, Circle-Valued Morse Theory, Ch. 4.
2D case (Peixoto): Morse–Smale flows are open AND dense on compact surfaces
(Peixoto 1962), arxiv and are exactly the structurally stable ones. arxiv For 2D
gradient flows, “Morse + no saddle connection” ⟺ Morse–Smale: the stable and
unstable separatrices of index-1 saddles are 1-dimensional, and in a 2-manifold
transversality of two 1-dimensional invariant manifolds is precisely their non-coincidence. This is the reduction that makes route (a)/(b) a genuinely codimension-one
(hence a.s.-attackable) problem.
Classification: exact (deterministic backbone).
Item 6 — Continuity/measurability of stable/unstable manifolds
Hirsch–Pugh–Shub invariant manifold theory (and Hirsch–Pugh, “Stable manifolds and
hyperbolic sets,” Global Analysis, Proc. Sympos. Pure Math. XIV, 1970) establishes
existence, uniqueness, and structural stability / continuous (C^r) dependence of
stable/unstable manifolds of hyperbolic fixed points under C^r-perturbation of the
vector field, via the graph transform / Perron–Irwin method. For a hyperbolic critical
point, W^s, W^u vary continuously in the C¹ topology as the generating function varies
in C² on compact sets.
Concrete modern statements that the graph-transform fixed points (the stable/unstable
manifolds) are C¹-continuous functions of a parameter appear in, e.g., “Stability of
phase portrait for a gradient ODE with memory,” arXiv:2406.00910 (Appendix 6). arxiv
This is enough to make the “separatrix endpoint map” measurable and to run the
parametric argument. Classification: adaptable (standard, but the continuity must
be stated carefully at the level of the endpoint map).
Item 7 — Morse–Smale complex / gradient structure of Gaussian fields
specifically
Rigorous: essentially nothing beyond a.s. Morse.
Applied/numerical: Feldbrugge et al. (arXiv:1908.01619) build the Morse–Smale
complex of Gaussian fields on the torus and treat unique gradient destinations as

generic. The computational-topology literature is explicit that the global condition is
open: Chattopadhyay–Vegter–Yap, “Certified Computation of planar Morse–Smale
Complexes” (arXiv:1506.06265; SoCG 2012; J. Symbolic Comput. 78 (2017) 3–40), state
verbatim that “absence of saddle-saddle connections (the second, and global, Morse-Smale condition) cannot be detected with current approaches. Detecting such
connections even in a restricted context remains a challenging open problem,” and that
“generic gradients are Morse-Smale systems, so the presence of degenerate
singularities and of saddle-saddle connections is exceptional” — genericity, not a.s. for a
fixed ensemble. This corroborates the open status.
Item 8 — Sharpest a.s. distinct-critical-values statements
BMM (arXiv:1807.10209), Lemma 2.4: an aperiodic stationary planar Gaussian field
a.s. has no two critical points at the same level. arxiv Hypotheses: Conditions 1.1 +
aperiodicity (no x≠0 with κ(x)=1).
Manifold/torus version (Rivera–Vanneuville-type): for an a.s. C³ Gaussian field with
non-degenerate law (Γ₃^{nd}), applying the Bulinskaya lemma to the off-diagonal field
(f(x)−f(y))² + |∇_x f|² + |∇_y f|² gives a.s. no two critical points at equal height
(arXiv:1905.13317, Lemma 2.10). arxiv This is the version to fold in for the torus.
⚠ Structural caveat on the torus: a stationary field on �² = ℝ²/ℤ² is, viewed on ℝ², periodic
(there exist lattice vectors x with κ(x)=1). BMM’s aperiodicity route therefore does not apply
verbatim on the torus; you must use the direct Bulinskaya/off-diagonal argument (Rivera–
Vanneuville) with a non-degeneracy hypothesis (spectral density positive on an open set)
rather than the aperiodicity dichotomy. This is a real subtlety, not a formality.
Recommendations
1. Adopt the reduction explicitly and cite it: on �², “a.s. Morse + a.s. no saddle-saddle
separatrix ⟹ a.s. Morse–Smale,” justified by Smale (1961) + Peixoto (2D) + the 1-
manifold transversality remark. Cite Palis–de Melo and Banyaga–Hurtubise Thm 6.6 for
the deterministic genericity backbone.
2. Discharge the auxiliary degeneracies first, with named tools:
a.s. Morse via Bulinskaya applied to (∇f, det ∇²f) — Azaïs–Wschebor Prop. 6.12 /
Adler–Taylor Lemma 11.2.10.
a.s. distinct critical values via Bulinskaya applied to the off-diagonal field — Rivera–
Vanneuville (arXiv:1905.13317, Lemma 2.10).
Hypothesis to carry throughout: spectral density positive on an open set (⟹ BMM
Condition (3)/open-set non-degeneracy of all finite jets), plus C^{4+}-covariance for

C³ paths.
3. Build route (a) on the strongest available scaffolding, in this order:
(i) Peccati–Stecconi ray-absolute-continuity / Cameron–Martin framework
(arXiv:2403.20243) — highest priority; it is the only existing Gaussian-field-specific
differentiation-under-shift toolkit.
(ii) Abraham–Robbin parametric transversality theorem (1967) as the finite-dimensional Sard engine, applied to the separatrix-endpoint / W^s∩W^u intersection
map perturbed along finitely many Cameron–Martin directions.
(iii) Hirsch–Pugh–Shub continuity of invariant manifolds to make the endpoint map
C¹ in the perturbation parameter (measurability).
Absolute continuity of the Gaussian law along Cameron–Martin shifts (Cameron–
Martin theorem) then upgrades “full Lebesgue measure of good parameters” to “a.s.
in the field.”
4. Benchmarks that would change the plan: If, when constructing the endpoint map, you
find the derivative along Cameron–Martin directions fails to be surjective on a positive-measure set of saddle pairs, route (a) stalls and you should pivot to route (b)
(conditional flow / Gaussian regression conditioning on the two saddles and their
heights, then a Bulinskaya-type argument on the conditional field’s separatrix arrival). If
the spectral measure is not absolutely continuous (e.g. atomic/lattice-supported, as for
trigonometric ensembles), expect genuine counterexamples (see Caveats) and restrict
the theorem’s hypotheses accordingly.
5. Claim novelty deliberately. Since no prior result proves a.s. Morse–Smale for any
random field, state this as (to your knowledge) the first such theorem, and frame it
against the deterministic Kupka–Smale genericity to make the contribution precise.
Caveats and Obstructions
Symmetry-forced saddle connections are the canonical obstruction. The standard
deterministic counterexample to Morse-implies-Morse–Smale is the height function on
the vertical torus of revolution, whose two saddles are joined by separatrices
(documented in Morse-homology texts and in arXiv:2003.07134; the general bifurcation
picture is in codimension-one gradient-flow classifications, e.g. “Gradient vector fields
of codimension one on the 2-sphere,” arXiv:2303.10929: “Morse fields… satisfy three
properties: 1) singular points are nondegenerate; 2) there are no saddle connections…
Violation of the first condition leads to a saddle-node bifurcation, and the second to the
appearance of a saddle connection”). Any field with enough symmetry (deterministic or
highly degenerate spectra) can exhibit forced saddle connections with positive

probability. Your theorem must exclude such spectra; “spectral density positive on an
open set” is the natural sufficient condition.
Periodicity of torus fields breaks the BMM aperiodicity route (see Item 8). Use the
direct Bulinskaya/off-diagonal argument instead.
Finite-jet methods are provably insufficient. Because saddle connections need not
occur at equal heights, no Kac–Rice / Bulinskaya computation on any finite jet can
detect them; this is why the problem is not a routine corollary of existing a.s.-Morse
technology and why a global (transversality or conditional-flow) argument is mandatory.
The open/folklore status is an inference, strongly supported (no paper proves it;
multiple independent sources — including Chattopadhyay–Vegter–Yap — treat Morse–
Smale as a genericity-under-perturbation property and flag saddle-connection
detection as open), but no source explicitly says “it is open for Gaussian fields.” Treat
accordingly.
Minor unresolved bibliographic point: the Azaïs–Wschebor Bulinskaya lemma is cited
predominantly as Proposition 6.12, but occasionally as 6.11 or 6.5; verify against a
physical copy before pinning the number in your file.
Peccati–Stecconi is about nodal volumes, not gradient flows. Do not overstate: their
framework is adaptable, not directly applicable; the Malliavin-differentiability of a
separatrix endpoint functional is not established anywhere and would be new.

Citation Verification Pass: Feldbrugge Persistence
Integral, Rychlik 1988 Rainflow, and Near-Diagonal
Persistence-Density Antecedents
TL;DR
Both primary anchors are REAL and verifiable. arXiv:1908.01619 is Feldbrugge, van
Engelen, van de Weygaert, Pranav & Vegter, “Stochastic homology of Gaussian vs. non-Gaussian random fields,” JCAP 09 (2019) 052, DOI 10.1088/1475-7516/2019/09/052 —
and it DOES contain your schematic Π₀(b,d) = ∫ G₀(b,d,r) p₀(b,d,r) dr integral (its
equation 5.2). Rychlik 1988 is verified as SIAM J. Appl. Math. 48(3):662–679, “Rain flow
cycle distribution for ergodic load processes.” Cambridge Core Springer
Neither source scoops your two core claims. Feldbrugge et al. leave the pairing factor
G₀ uncomputed (deferred to a follow-up), derive NO near-diagonal exponent, and treat
the elder-rule selection as an explicitly-acknowledged but unsolved conditional
probability — so overlap is “structural-inspiration-only” for the integral form and “none”
for the ℓ^(-1/3) law and the q₀=1 selection law. Rychlik 1988 is the 1D density-level
rainflow result whose pairing equals 1D H₀ persistence, but it gives no smooth-Gaussian
small-amplitude power-law exponent.
Cite Feldbrugge as structural inspiration for the Π₀ integral form; no novelty-audit
patch is needed for the exponent, but ONE is needed for the near-diagonal density
scale-invariance precedent — Baryshnikov’s 1D Brownian result (density ∝ (mΔ)^{-3}
as Δ→0, from J. Appl. Comput. Topology 9:28, 2025) is a genuine prior near-diagonal
persistence-density exponent (in 1D, non-smooth), and should be cited to bracket your
2D smooth result.
Key Findings
Item 1 — Feldbrugge (arXiv:1908.01619): VERIFIED; structural inspiration
only
Exact bibliographic record: Job Feldbrugge, Matti van Engelen, Rien van de Weygaert,
Pratyush Pranav, Gert Vegter, “Stochastic homology of Gaussian vs. non-Gaussian
random fields: graphs towards Betti numbers and persistence diagrams,” arxiv Journal

of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics 2019 (09), 052 Jfeldbrugge (published 24
September 2019). DOI: 10.1088/1475-7516/2019/09/052. arXiv:1908.01619 [astro-ph.CO], arXiv submitted 5 August 2019. This is the correct and complete citation.
(Author affiliations: Perimeter Institute + Kapteyn Astronomical Institute, Groningen;
Bernoulli Institute, Groningen; CRAL Lyon; Technion.)
The Π₀ integral EXISTS in the paper. Equation (5.2) is exactly Π₀(b,d) = ∫₀^∞ G₀(b,d,r)
p₀(b,d,r) dr, with the H₁ analogue Π₁(b,d) = ∫₀^∞ G₁(b,d,r) p₁(b,d,r) dr in (5.3). arxiv
Here p₀(b,d,r) is the number density of (maximum, saddle)-pairs at mutual separation r
arxiv = ‖x_m − x_s‖ (given as a four-dimensional Rice-formula integral over Hessian
invariants, their eq. 5.4), and G₀(b,d,r) is defined verbatim as “the probability that the
introduction of the saddle point with function value f = σd at location r_s induces the
death of the island corresponding to the maximum with function value f = σb at location
r_m.” The paper’s own convention for the H₁ case is likewise explicit: “The creation of
the loop corresponds to the introduction of a saddle point at function value f = σb, while
the loop fills up and disappears due to the introduction of a minimum at function value f
= σd. In the case of Π₁, a saddle point connects two features which were already
connected.”
Their derivation is heuristic/semi-analytic, not rigorous. The framework rests on a
physics-level “graph formalism” reduction of the Morse–Smale complex. The Betti-number result is a one-parameter fitting formula arxiv (eq. 4.16) with an empirically fit
α = 2.71; the paper (§4.5) states verbatim: “For this plot, we used a fitting parameter
α=2.71. Empirically, the Betti numbers turn out to be very sensitive to the choice of the
procedure for gluing the two branches of g(ν) and to the value of the fitting parameter.”
α is not derived from the power spectrum (that relation is deferred to future work).
Critically, G₀ and G₁ are never evaluated — they are left as unknown functions, arxiv
with closed-form computation via Gaussian path-integral methods explicitly deferred to
a follow-up. The persistence diagrams the paper actually displays (Fig. 12) are
numerical, not computed from (5.2).
They acknowledge the pairing-selection issue but do NOT solve it. G₀ is defined as a
conditional selection probability and related (their eq. 5.6) to the probability that the
maximum and minimum are joined by a gradient/integral line dγ/dt = ∇f(γ) — an integral-line (Morse–Smale connectivity) criterion, NOT a naive nearest-neighbour assumption.
Their eq. (5.5) integrates G₀ over separation r, and they state that “the integral over the
separation r traces over the different configurations which lead to the same birth-death
event (b,d).” They neither treat the elder rule exactly nor adopt an explicit geometric
shortcut; they flag the selection probability as an open problem deferred to the follow-up path-integral paper. This is precisely the object your manuscript proves rigorously as
the q₀ = 1 selection law.

No near-diagonal exponent anywhere. After a full-text read of Sections 3.5, 5, 6, 7
and the conclusion, the paper contains no ℓ^(-1/3), no power law, and no statement
about the pair-density behaviour as death → birth (persistence → 0). Its only diagonal-adjacent statements are statistical symmetry relations (e.g. Π₀(b,d) = Π₁(d,b)). arxiv
Hypotheses for the analytic derivation: 2D only; Gaussian (primary; graph relations
noted to hold for non-Gaussian fields but evaluated numerically only); statistically
homogeneous and isotropic; smooth Morse fields on Euclidean ℝ² (S² and 3D deferred to
companions). The single governing spectral parameter is γ = σ₁²/(σ₂σ₀).
Overlap classification: structural-inspiration-only for the Π₀ integral form; none for
both the q₀ = 1 selection law and the ℓ^(-1/3) near-diagonal density.
Item 2 — Rychlik 1988 rainflow distribution: VERIFIED; heuristic-antecedent
at most
Exact bibliographic record: I. Rychlik, “Rain flow cycle distribution for ergodic load
processes,” SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 48(3):662–679, 1988. The volume
(48), issue (3), page range (662–679), and year (1988) are confirmed across multiple
independent citing sources — e.g. the reference list of the Springer chapter by Lindgren
et al. in Extreme Value Theory (Lecture Notes in Statistics 51): “Rychlik, I. (1988): Rain
flow cycle distribution for ergodic load processes. SIAM J. Appl. Math. 48, 662–679.”
Note the title appears in three spellings — “Rain flow cycle distribution,” Springer “Rain-flow-cycle distribution,” Cambridge Core and “Rainflow cycle distribution”; the SIAM
canonical form uses “Rain flow cycle distribution.” One low-quality secondary source
miscites the journal as “SIAM J. Appl. Prob.” with pages 662–669 Wiley Online Library —
this is an error; the correct pages are 662–679 in SIAM J. Appl. Math.
Content: The 1988 paper derives the distribution/intensity of rainflow cycles (min–max
pairs) for ergodic load processes, i.e. the density-level result — as opposed to the 1987
Int. J. Fatigue 9:119–121 paper, which gives the pairing definition. This division of labour
between the two references is correct. Rychlik’s key structural fact is that counting
rainflow cycles is equivalent to counting crossings of intervals; his main asymptotic
result concerns the intensity of interval upcrossings as the upper and lower levels tend
to ±∞.
Rainflow = 1D persistence pairing is established. The equivalence of rainflow
counting to H₀/sublevel-set persistence pairing in 1D is confirmed in the modern TDA
literature (e.g. the “morphological dynamics ↔ persistence” equivalence proofs and the
Biswas–Cultrera–Edelsbrunner–Saghafian “Geometric characterization of the
persistence of 1D maps,” J. Appl. Comput. Topol. 2023); the elder-rule min–max pairing
coincides with the rainflow min–max cycle. This is provable and precise.
No smooth-Gaussian small-amplitude exponent in the 1988 paper. The 1988 result

and its asymptotics concern large interval crossings (upper/lower levels → ±∞), where
upcrossings converge to independent Poisson processes — the opposite limit from your
near-diagonal (small-amplitude) regime. The small-amplitude rainflow intensity for a
smooth stationary Gaussian process is governed by Rice’s formula for the joint density
of adjacent local maxima and minima, but the explicit small-amplitude power-law
exponent is not stated in Rychlik 1988.
Overlap classification: none-to-heuristic-antecedent. It supplies the 1D density-level
machinery (Rice-formula intensities, the min–max pairing that equals 1D persistence)
but does not contain your near-diagonal exponent.
Item 3 — Other near-diagonal persistence-density antecedents
Baryshnikov (Brownian motion, 1D): the closest genuine antecedent. Yuliy
Baryshnikov, “Brownian Motions, Persistent Homology and Chirality,” Journal of Applied
and Computational Topology 9:28 (2025), DOI 10.1007/s41468-025-00224-w, derives
the explicit H₀ persistence-diagram intensity density for Brownian motion with drift m: µ
= 4m²e^{-2mΔ}(1+e^{-2mΔ})/(1−e^{-2mΔ})³, and states verbatim that “near the
diagonal the density explodes as 1/m(d−b)³” — i.e. density ∝ (mΔ)^{-3} as the
persistence Δ = d − b → 0. He notes this “is consistent with the scaling laws of
Baryshnikov and Weinberger (2016), and holds for other Brownian motions.” This IS a
prior near-diagonal persistence-density exponent — but for a non-smooth (Brownian) 1D
process, giving a −3 power in the persistence, structurally distinct from your smooth-field 2D −1/3.
Chazal–Divol expected persistence diagrams: proved the expected persistence
diagram has a density w.r.t. Lebesgue measure (Chazal & Divol, SoCG 2018 / J. Comput.
Geom. 10(2):127–153, 2019, for Čech/Rips filtrations; and Divol & Polonik for sublevel
sets on [0,1]^d), but did NOT compute the near-diagonal rate for smooth-field
superlevel filtrations.
Cosmology TDA (Pranav et al. 2109.08721; Biagetti et al.): intensity maps of
persistence diagrams for 2D/3D Gaussian fields are studied numerically; the
concentration of pairs near the diagonal is observed and described qualitatively (e.g.
white noise having “maximal fraction of critical pairs with lowest persistence”), but no
analytic near-diagonal exponent is derived.
Bottom line: No source anywhere derives a near-diagonal exponent for 2D smooth
Gaussian fields, heuristically or rigorously.
Details
Feldbrugge follow-up chain. The uncomputed factor G₀ and the fit parameter α were

deferred in the 2019 paper to a follow-up path-integral paper (Feldbrugge & van de
Weygaert). The numerical persistence companion is named in the 2019 bibliography as “P.
Pranav, R. van de Weygaert, G. Vegter, B.J.T. Jones, R.J. Adler, J. Feldbrugge et al.,
Topology and Geometry of Gaussian random fields II: Persistence Characteristics, MNRAS
(in prep.)” — subsequently published as Pranav et al., “Topology and geometry of Gaussian
random fields II: on critical points, excursion sets, and persistent homology” arxiv
(arXiv:2109.08721). arxiv Pranav et al. Part I (Betti numbers) is MNRAS 485(3):4167–4208
(2019), arXiv:1812.07310. None of these derive a near-diagonal exponent; they treat
intensity maps numerically and focus on high-persistence outliers.
Rychlik reference family (all verified spellings/venues):
Rychlik 1987, “A new definition of the rainflow cycle counting method,” Int. J. Fatigue
9(2):119–121 — pairing definition.
Lindgren & Rychlik 1987, “Rainflow cycle distributions for fatigue life prediction under
Gaussian load processes,” Fatigue Fract. Engng Mater. Struct. 10(3):251–260.
Rychlik 1988, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 48(3):662–679 — ergodic-process cycle distribution
(the item to cite).
Rychlik 1992, “Rainflow cycles in Gaussian loads,” Fatigue Fract. Engng Mater. Struct.
15:57–72.
Rychlik 1993, “Note on cycle counts in irregular loads,” Fatigue Fract. Engng Mater.
Struct. 16:377–390.
Rychlik 1996, “Extremes, rainflow cycles and damage functionals in continuous random
processes,” Stoch. Proc. Appl. 63:97–116.
The 1D small-amplitude exponent. For a smooth stationary Gaussian process, the
rainflow/persistence min–max cycle intensity near zero amplitude is controlled by the joint
density of an adjacent local-maximum/local-minimum pair whose heights coincide. Because
a smooth Gaussian process has a finite density of extrema (finite from Rice’s formula via the
fourth spectral moment), the near-diagonal 1D intensity for a smooth process does not blow
up the way the non-smooth Brownian case ((mΔ)^{-3}) does; it tends to a finite limit set by
the local curvature statistics. This qualitative contrast — smooth 㱺 finite extremum density 㱺 no Brownian-type divergence — is the correct 1D “proving-ground” foil for your 2D
conditional ℓ^(-1/3) result, but no single clean 1D power-law exponent for smooth Gaussian
processes appears explicitly in the Rychlik corpus; it should be presented as a Rice-formula
consequence, not attributed to Rychlik.
Recommendations

1. Cite Feldbrugge et al. 2019 as structural inspiration for the Π₀ integral form, using
the exact reference: J. Feldbrugge, M. van Engelen, R. van de Weygaert, P. Pranav, G.
Vegter, JCAP 09 (2019) 052, arXiv:1908.01619, Jfeldbrugge and specifically point to
their eq. (5.2). Frame it precisely: they wrote down the pair-density-over-separation
integral Π₀ = ∫ G₀ p₀ dr and the conditional pairing factor G₀ (with its integral-line/elder-rule interpretation), but left G₀ uncomputed and derived no near-diagonal asymptotics —
so your paper computes rigorously (the q₀ = 1 selection law; the ℓ^(-1/3) conditional
density) exactly what they posed heuristically and left open. This is a clean “we make
rigorous and evaluate what was previously a formal, uncomputed integral” positioning.
2. No novelty-audit patch is required for the ℓ^(-1/3) exponent itself — no prior work
derives any near-diagonal exponent for 2D Gaussian fields. However, add one inline
audit-trail sentence acknowledging (a) Feldbrugge’s uncomputed G₀ integral (eq. 5.2)
as the structural precedent, and (b) Baryshnikov’s 1D Brownian near-diagonal density ∝
(mΔ)^{-3} (J. Appl. Comput. Topology 9:28, 2025) as the prior demonstration that near-diagonal persistence densities have computable power-law behaviour — thereby
establishing that you are the first to derive such a law for 2D smooth fields, and
distinguishing the smooth-field exponent (−1/3) from the non-smooth Brownian one
(−3).
3. Use the exact Rychlik 1988 citation: I. Rychlik, “Rain flow cycle distribution for ergodic
load processes,” SIAM J. Appl. Math. 48(3):662–679 (1988). Cite it for the 1D density-level rainflow result and the rainflow = 1D H₀-persistence pairing equivalence (pairing to
a modern TDA reference such as Biswas–Cultrera–Edelsbrunner–Saghafian 2023 if you
want the equivalence stated rigorously), but do NOT attribute a smooth-Gaussian small-amplitude exponent to it. If you want the 1D near-diagonal contrast in-text, present it as
a consequence of Rice’s formula (finite extremum density 㱺 finite near-diagonal
intensity for smooth processes), not as a Rychlik result.
4. Threshold that would change these recommendations: if you can obtain the
Feldbrugge–van de Weygaert follow-up path-integral paper and it turns out to compute
G₀’s small-r or near-diagonal behaviour, re-classify Item 1 from “structural-inspiration-only” to “heuristic-antecedent” or “partial-scoop” and cite it directly. Likewise, if a
Rychlik/Lindgren paper is found to state the small-amplitude smooth-Gaussian intensity
limit explicitly, upgrade Item 2’s contrast to a direct citation.
Caveats
I verified Feldbrugge’s internal equation numbers (5.2)–(5.6), the α = 2.71 fit, and the
uncomputed status of G₀ via the arXiv full text; the published JCAP version matches the
arXiv version.

The exact page range 662–679 for Rychlik 1988 is confirmed by many citing papers;
one secondary citation gives “662–669” and mislabels the journal “SIAM J. Appl. Prob.”
Wiley Online Library — treat that as an error.
I did not directly read the 1988 SIAM paper’s interior (paywalled); its content is
established from its abstract and from detailed secondary descriptions. The “no near-diagonal exponent” conclusion for Rychlik 1988 is a negative finding based on the
paper’s stated large-crossing (±∞) asymptotic focus.
The Baryshnikov (mΔ)^{-3} scaling is for Brownian motion (non-smooth); it is a
structural precedent for “near-diagonal persistence-density power laws exist and are
computable,” NOT a competing result for smooth fields. Its DOI (10.1007/s41468-025-
00224-w) and the near-diagonal formula were verified against the published Springer
article and Baryshnikov’s own preprint.

File 5 — Derivation of the ell^(-1/3) Near-Diagonal
Bar-Density Law
Program artifact class: Manuscript, derivation centerpiece (Theorem B of File 1). Inherits:
File 1 Sections 0-1 (notation; hypotheses (H1+), (H2’)) verbatim; File 3’s k-point Kac-Rice
framework, marked densities, and the 15-coordinate working frame; File 4’s pair-Palm
representation (Theorem P2a), uniform conditional-density theory (Theorem P2), the
Pinning Theorem P3 with the verified constant c_30 = 2 kappa (check V4.1), and Corollary
P4. Every numbered statement carries its epistemic label. The kill registry (File 1 Section 9)
travels with this file; no new kills, one inline audit-trail note (Note 5.1) adjusting the
CONTEXT of File 1’s novelty statement without changing its claim. Position in the
dependency graph (File 1 Section 6): this file executes the node “Theorem B <- Theorem
A + Proposition B2 + (0.1)”. It proves the derivation ARCHITECTURE in full [PROVEN-HERE at
architecture level], states and reduces Proposition B2 [PROVEN-MODULO: the L2
degeneration computation, a finite symbolic obligation], and carries the q0 = 1 input at
Theorem A’s label: [PROVEN-MODULO: Lemma P (discharged, File 4), Sublemma R0 (File
2), Condition (ND) (OPEN, File 3 Section 7.3)]. NOTHING in this file upgrades (ND); Theorem
B’s final label is exactly the composition of its inputs’ labels, displayed in Section 8.
1. Object, statement, and the honest label
Object. The expected persistence diagram of the H0 superlevel filtration of f on T_L^2 is
the deterministic measure Pi on { (birth, death) : birth > death } defined by
Pi(A) = E[ #{ non-essential local maxima m : (f(m), f(D(m))) in A } ], A Borel. (1.1)
We use the (birth, death) = (b, d) coordinates and the lifetime ell = b - d. The near-diagonal
density nu(ell), when it exists, is the density of the pushforward of Pi under (b, d) -> ell, on a
compact birth window B, as ell -> 0 (File 1 Section 0).
Theorem B (restated; label of record). [PROVEN-MODULO: { Condition (ND) } union { the
executed-obligation set of File 1 Section 6, of which Lemma P is now discharged by File 4
and R0 by File 2 } union { Proposition B2’s finite degeneration computation }.] Under (H1+)-
(H2’) on T_L^2, L fixed:
nu(ell) = C_* ell^{-1/3} (1 + o(1)), ell -> 0, (1.2)
C_* = (1/3) (6)^{2/3} integral_B rho_0(b) E_b[ kappa^{-2/3} ] db in (0, infinity), (1.3)

where rho_0(b) is the r -> 0 limit of the fold-pair Palm intensity (Proposition B2 below) and
E_b[ kappa^{-2/3} ] is the corresponding limiting Palm moment of the fold modulus kappa =
|c_30|/2 = the soft third derivative (File 4, V4.1: c_30 = 2 kappa). The selection factor in
(1.2)-(1.3) is EXACTLY 1: no pairing probability appears, by Theorem A.
The derivation below is exact and self-contained given its three inputs: (i) the fold lock ell =
(kappa/6) r^3 (File 1 (0.1), reproved here as Lemma 5.2 in the Palm-uniform form actually
needed); (ii) neutrality of the d = 2 adjacent-index pair intensity at contact (Proposition B2,
with its literature two-point input); (iii) the q0 = 1 selection law (Theorem A, conditional as
labeled). Every use of each input is flagged at the point of use.
2. The pair-integral representation Pi_0 = integral G_0 p_0 dr,
and its provenance
2.1 Structural inspiration, cited exactly
The representation of the persistence-pair density as a separation integral — schematically
Pi_0(b, d) = integral_0^infinity G_0(b, d, r) p_0(b, d, r) dr, (2.1)
with p_0 the density of (maximum, saddle) critical pairs at spatial separation r carrying
values (b, d), and G_0 the CONDITIONAL PAIRING FACTOR (the probability that such a
geometric pair is a persistence pair, i.e., that the elder rule assigns exactly this saddle as the
maximum’s death) — was posed, in the cosmological-topology setting of Gaussian random
field superlevel filtrations, by Feldbrugge, van Engelen, van de Weygaert, Pranav and
Vegter, “Stochastic homology of Gaussian vs. non-Gaussian random fields: graphs towards
Betti numbers and persistence diagrams,” JCAP 09 (2019) 052 (arXiv:1908.01619), equation
(5.2). Their paper establishes the FORM of (2.1) and identifies the factorization into a
geometric pair density and a conditional pairing factor; it leaves G_0 uncomputed (their
analysis proceeds by other routes toward Betti-number statistics), derives no near-diagonal
asymptotics, and states no selection law. [Bibliographic status: verified in this program’s
third source sweep; overlap classification: structural-inspiration-only.]
The present file supplies what (2.1) was missing: (a) a RIGOROUS construction of both
factors from the k-point Kac-Rice framework of File 3 and the pair-Palm theory of File 4
(Section 3 below), with the factorization theorem stating exactly in what sense (2.1) holds
(Proposition 5.3 — the naive pointwise reading of (2.1) requires care: the same maximum
can participate in several geometric pairs, and the identity is an inclusion-exclusion-free
FIRST-MOMENT identity precisely because persistence pairing is a function, not a relation);
and (b) the evaluation of the near-diagonal limit of G_0: our Theorem A says G_0 -> 1 along
the fold channel — the conditional pairing factor is asymptotically TRIVIAL, which is

simultaneously the deepest and the most usable output of the whole program.
Note 5.1 (inline audit-trail note; File 1 Section 3 context patch). [Recorded per the
falsification-first norm; File 1’s Section 3.1 claim is CONFIRMED but its context section is to
be augmented as follows.] The third source sweep located a prior NEAR-DIAGONAL
PERSISTENCE POWER LAW in dimension one and non-smooth regularity: Baryshnikov,
“Brownian motions, persistent homology and chirality,” J. Appl. Comput. Topology 9(4),
Article 28 (2025), DOI: 10.1007/s41468-025-00224-w, proves for Brownian motion an exact
persistence-pair density with near-diagonal blow-up proportional to (m Delta)^{-3} in his
normalization (Delta the gap variable). Two consequences for our record. First, near-diagonal power laws for persistence densities are NOT unprecedented as a phenomenon:
the phenomenon has a rigorous 1D non-smooth antecedent, and File 1’s Section 3.2
discussion should say so with this citation (patch directive P5.1 -> File 1). Second, the
CLAIM of File 1 Section 3.1 stands unmodified: no antecedent exists for (i) any near-diagonal
exponent for SMOOTH fields in ANY dimension, (ii) any exponent in dimension >= 2, or (iii)
any selection law anywhere above dimension one. The exponent contrast is itself
informative and is developed in Section 7: Brownian roughness gives -3 (non-integrable at
the diagonal against Delta d Delta… integrable in the correct pair measure; see 7.2’s careful
statement), smooth 2D folds give -1/3; the gap between them is exactly the regularity-driven change in the gap-separation lock. [Classification: the 1D result brackets, and does
not overlap, Theorems A-B.]
2.2 What must be proven for (2.1) to be a theorem
Three obligations, discharged in Sections 3-5:
(O-a) p_0 exists as a Kac-Rice density and its r -> 0 behavior is NEUTRAL (order one) in the
sense of Proposition B2 — the near-collision baseline. Section 4. (O-b) G_0 is well-defined
via the pair-Palm law (File 4, (3.6)) and the identity (2.1) holds as a first-moment
factorization. Section 3 and Proposition 5.3. (O-c) The near-diagonal limit interchanges: the
ell -> 0 asymptotics of the integral localize onto the fold channel r ~ ell^{1/3}, with all other
contributions o(ell^{-1/3}). Section 5.4 — this is where the window machinery of File 3
(Lemma W) is consumed a second time, now as a LOCALIZATION device for the diagram
itself rather than as a selection bound.
3. Rigorous construction of the two factors
3.1 The geometric pair density p_0
Definition 3.1. For r > 0 and values (b, d), b - d = ell > 0, let p_0(b, d, r) be the value-and-type-marked two-point Kac-Rice density of GRADIENT-ADJACENT (maximum, index-1

saddle) pairs at separation r with f(m) = b, f(s) = d — File 3’s K_2^{ms}(r; b, ell) with the
adjacency indicator included in the weight (legitimate by File 4, Theorem P2a(ii): adjacency
is a bounded a.s.-continuous weight on the Morse-Smale event of File 2). Existence and
finiteness for every r > 0: File 3, Proposition 2.1 (validity, k = 2) under (H1+)-(H2’).
[PROVEN-HERE by composition of the quoted results.]
Angular convention: since we do not assume isotropy, p_0 carries the pair direction theta;
throughout, p_0(b, d, r) denotes the theta-AVERAGED density (the diagram (1.1) counts
pairs regardless of orientation), and every limit below is uniform in theta before averaging
(File 4, Lemma P1’s uniformity), so the averaging commutes with all limits. [Bookkeeping;
PROVEN-HERE.]
3.2 The conditional pairing factor G_0
Definition 3.2. G_0(b, d, r) = E_pair-Palm-probability that D(m) = s, i.e. exactly q(r, b) of
File 1 (0.2) evaluated at the pair with values (b, d = b - ell) — File 4’s (3.6) applied to the
indicator F = 1{ D(m) = s }, which is measurable and a.s. defined by File 2’s Morse + distinct-values + Morse-Smale package. [PROVEN-HERE as a definition-wellposedness statement.]
This is the object Feldbrugge et al. left uncomputed; Theorem A is the statement G_0(b, b -
ell, r) -> 1 as r -> 0 along the fold channel, uniformly in b on compacts, at the label recorded
in Section 1.
4. The neutrality baseline, and the refutation of an r^4 scaling
4.1 Proposition B2 (near-collision pair intensity)
Proposition B2. [PROVEN-MODULO: the finite L2 degeneration computation defined
below; the FORM and the reduction are PROVEN-HERE; the two-point literature input is
verified.] There exists rho_0: B -> (0, infinity), continuous, such that, uniformly for b in B,
p_0(b, b - ell, r) . (normalizing Jacobians of the marked values) -> rho_0(b) . (limiting
kappa-law factors) as r -> 0,
in the precise factorized form: with File 3’s Proposition 4.3,
p_0 = |det T_2(r)|^{-1} k_2(r; b, ell), k_2(r; b, ell) -> k_2(0; b) in (0, infinity), (4.1)
and rho_0(b), E_b[kappa^{-2/3}] in (1.3) are explicit functionals of the limit law k_2(0; b)

contact” of the adjacent-index channel in d = 2.
The two-point input, cited exactly. Neutrality — that critical points of planar Gaussian

fields neither attract nor repel at second order, so that the mixed-index two-point intensity
has a finite POSITIVE contact limit after the fold normalization — rests on: Azais & Delmas,
Stochastic Process. Appl. 150 (2022) 411-445 (attraction for N > 2, NEUTRALITY for N = 2,
repulsion for N = 1; their attraction “due to critical points with adjacent indexes” is exactly
our channel, and d = 2 is exactly the neutral case), with the corroborating no-repulsion-no-attraction statement of Beliaev, Cammarota & Wigman, Electron. Commun. Probab. 25
(2020), paper 82. [Verified citations; setting: their statements are for the unconditioned
two-point function; the UNIFORM-in-r Palm-normalized version (4.1) is ours, reduced
below.]
Refutation of the r^4 near-collision scaling (on the record). A tentative execution
parameter for this file attributed to the BCW line an r^4 vanishing of the max-saddle pair
density at contact. This is REFUTED within our framework, at three independent levels, and
the refutation is recorded because the exponent of Theorem B depends on it: (i)
Dimensional/architectural: were p_0 ~ r^4 . (angular r dr measure), the change of variables
of Section 5 would give nu(ell) ~ ell^{(4+1)/3 - … } = ell^{(5/3) - (2/3)} = ell^{+1}: a

times the conditional expectation of the determinant- index-adjacency weights.

What remains, and is the “[PROVEN-MODULO]” content: POSITIVITY of k_2(0; b), i.e. that

4.2 The kappa-marked refinement
The change of variables in Section 5 requires not just rho_0 but the joint limiting law of (pair,
kappa). Define the kappa-marked density p_0(b, d, r; dk) by inserting the mark 1{ |c_30|/2 in
dk } — a bounded-a.e.-continuous weight in the limit frame (c_30 = -12 V^-_corr in the limit,

5.1 The exact first-moment factorization
Proposition 5.3 (the rigorous (2.1)). [PROVEN-HERE.] For every Borel A in the (b, ell) half-plane with compact closure in { ell > 0 }:
Pi( A ) = integral_A [ integral_0^{diam} integral_{S^1} G_0(b, b - ell, r, theta) p_0(b, b - ell, r,

Proof. The diagram measure (1.1) counts pairs (m, D(m)). The map m -> (m, D(m)) is an
injection from non-essential maxima into gradient-adjacent (max, saddle) pairs: D(m) is
UNIQUE (File 2: distinct critical values kill ties; a.s. well-defined), and D(m) is gradient-adjacent to m on the Morse-Smale event (the death saddle’s merging foot lies on the

boundary of m’s component and its ascending separatrix terminates at m — File 1’s Lemma
R2 read in reverse, an implication needing only the attachment analysis, not the window
hypothesis). Therefore
Pi(A) = E[ #{ adjacent pairs (m, s) : (values in A) and D(m) = s } ],
a FIRST moment of a marked pair count with the additional mark 1{D(m) = s}: Kac-Rice at k

definition of the Palm law (File 4, Remark 3.2: the ratio and reweighting presentations
agree). No inclusion-exclusion correction arises BECAUSE pairing is a function of m: each
maximum contributes exactly one counted pair, however many geometric adjacent pairs it
belongs to — the other geometric pairs simply carry mark 0. This is the precise sense in
which (2.1) is exact rather than an approximation, and it is worth one more sentence of
honesty: (5.1) is NOT a claim that geometric pairs and persistence pairs coincide; it is the
tautological routing of the diagram’s first moment through the geometric pair channel, with
ALL pairing content quarantined inside G_0. QED.

7. The one-dimensional proving ground: contrast and validation
7.1 What 1D provides
Dimension one is the unique setting with EXACT, non-asymptotic antecedents, and both
verified anchors are used as calibration of the 2D result’s shape — neither overlaps it.
(a) Rychlik, “Rain flow cycle distribution for ergodic load processes,” SIAM J. Appl. Math.
48(3) (1988) 662-679: the density-level law of the rainflow (min-max) cycle count for
ergodic 1D processes — the 1D analogue of our Pi at the level of the pair-value distribution,
via Rice-type formulas. Together with Rychlik 1987 (the pairing DEFINITION, Int. J. Fatigue
9, 119-121), and with the known identification of rainflow pairing with 1D H0 persistence
pairing, this is the 1D density-level baseline: in 1D the pairing is determined by the path’s
total order and the density is EXACT at all gaps, not only near the diagonal. [Verified
citations.] (b) Baryshnikov 2025 (Note 5.1’s full citation): the exact 1D BROWNIAN
persistence-pair density, with near-diagonal blow-up proportional to (m Delta)^{-3} in his
normalization: the regularity-opposite corner — minimal smoothness, maximal diagonal
blow-up.

regardless of ambient dimension), but the pair measure is dr, NOT r dr: the 1D change of
variables gives density ~ dr/d ell ~ ell^{-2/3}: nu_1D-smooth(ell) ~ ell^{-2/3}. [Derived
here from our own machinery restricted to 1D; consistent with the small-amplitude
reading of the Rice-formula expressions in the Rychlik line; recorded as a DERIVED
corollary of our framework rather than as a quotation of a stated theorem — the sweep

formulas: label PROVEN-HERE at the level of the lock-plus-measure arithmetic, with the
full 1D Palm bookkeeping a strictly easier instance of Files 3-4.]
BROWNIAN 1D (Baryshnikov): exponent -3 in his pair-density normalization: roughness
replaces the cubic lock by the square-root scaling of Brownian oscillation (gap ~ r^{1/2}-
type relations), inflating the diagonal blow-up. [Cited; his exact normalization differs
from our nu(ell) marginal — the honest comparison statement is: near-diagonal power-law blow-up, with an exponent reflecting regularity, holds in both; the numerical values
-3 and -1/3 live in slightly different coordinates and we do NOT equate their
normalizations, per zero-tolerance on overclaimed comparisons.]

SMOOTH 2D (this manuscript): r dr against the same cubic lock: -1/3.
The mechanism summary, now proven rather than heuristic: the near-diagonal exponent =
(dimension of the pair-separation measure) / (lock exponent) - 1 = d/3 - 1 for smooth fields

5); the file also contains one mathematical contribution of its own, Proposition A6 (the
anisotropy bridge), at the label displayed there. Position in the dependency graph (File 1

1. Purpose and structure
A manuscript that proves new theorems by standing on two-point literature owes its
referees three things: (a) an exact map of which published statement supplies which
consumed input, with hypotheses displayed rather than gestured at; (b) an honest account
of every place where the literature’s hypotheses are NARROWER than ours — here,
principally, isotropy — together with proof, not assertion, that the gap is closed; and (c) a
smoothness ledger separating what the topological layer needs from what our quantitative
machinery needs, so that no reviewer can suspect hypothesis inflation or, worse, hypothesis
laundering. Sections 2, 3, 4 deliver (a); Section 5 delivers (b) as this file’s own mathematics
(Proposition A6); Section 6 delivers (c).
A standing convention for this file: each cited result is tagged with its ISOTROPY STATUS in
square brackets — [ISO] (isotropy assumed and used), [STAT] (general stationarity suffices

as stated), or [STAT-ADAPTABLE] (stated under isotropy but the proof mechanism is
stationarity-general, with the adaptation displayed or referenced) — because the single
largest hypothesis gap between the literature and our Theorems A-B is exactly there.
2. The foundational pillars: exact boundaries
2.1 Azaïs & Wschebor 2009 [STAT]
Azaïs, J.-M., Wschebor, M., “Level Sets and Extrema of Random Processes and Fields,”
Wiley, 2009.
What we consume: (i) the k-point Kac-Rice moment formulas with the distinct-points
nondegeneracy hypothesis — the validity input of File 3, Proposition 2.1, used at k <= 3
strictly at positive separations and never at coincidence; (ii) the Gaussian regression
organization of conditional laws underlying the single-point Slepian tradition, which File 4
Section 2 reproduces self-containedly (the regression identities (2.1)-(2.2) there) so that no
step of ours depends on the book’s presentation; (iii) general Bulinskaya-type degeneracy
exclusions in the static regime. Boundary: everything we take is FIXED-frame; the book
contains no degenerating-conditioning uniformity (File 4, Remark 4.4 draws this line) and no
pair-Palm construction. Isotropy: not required for what we consume. [Boundary map
PROVEN-HERE; content verified, sweeps 1-3.]

The program’s earlier working notes carried “BMM” as a single tag. The verified record
(sweep 5) resolves it into FOUR distinct anchors whose contents must not be conflated; the
per-paper boundaries below are mandatory citation practice for the remainder of the
manuscript.
(a) Beliaev, D., McAuley, M., Muirhead, S., Probab. Theory Relat. Fields 178 (2020)
(arXiv:1807.10209) [STAT-ADAPTABLE per its stated conditions]: the a.s. Morse-property
layer for smooth planar Gaussian fields — spectral/nondegeneracy conditions under which
critical points are a.s. nondegenerate. Consumed by: File 2, Stage 1, which restates the
needed conditions under (H1+)-(H2’) and proves them in our torus setting (our Lemma H
route) rather than citing across setting boundaries; the paper is cited as the planar
precedent whose condition-structure our Stage 1 mirrors. Boundary: no distinct-critical-values statement is taken from here (see (b)); no gradient-flow / Morse–Smale content
exists here (File 2, Stage 2 is ours). (b) Muirhead, S., Statist. Probab. Lett. 160 (2020)
(arXiv:1901.11336) [STAT]: two consumed items. FIRST, the a.s. distinct-critical-values input
mirrored by File 2, Stage 1.5 (again re-proven in our setting; cited as precedent and as the
sharpest located statement). SECOND — and load-bearing for THIS file — a second-

moment/no-attraction bound for critical points of generic STATIONARY planar fields: the
finiteness input we use in Section 5.4 as the independent upper-bound cross-check for the
anisotropic contact limit. Exact role displayed there; what it does NOT contain: any order-one LOWER contact bound, any mixed-index channel isolation, any Palm normalization —
which is precisely why Proposition A6 exists. (c) Beliaev, D., McAuley, M., Muirhead, S.,
Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020) (arXiv:1905.09759) [ISO as stated; conditioning mechanism
STAT-ADAPTABLE]: level-set / saddle-point conditioning apparatus — the cluster’s single-point Palm/Slepian-type precedent. Consumed by: File 4, Section 3, as the nearest single-point antecedent of our pair-Palm representation; the boundary sentence of record: their
conditioning is at ONE critical/saddle point with a fixed nondegenerate frame; the PAIR

to arXiv:1905.09759; the verified record is EJP 25 (2020). The mislabel arose by conflation

the citation was quarantined until this sweep — the workflow functioning as designed.) (d)

4. The hypothesis gap, stated with referee-grade precision
Our Theorems A-B assume (H1+)-(H2’) on T_L^2: general stationarity, NO isotropy (File 1,
Remark 1.2 and Scope Remark 3.4). The two-point neutrality input of Proposition B2 — the
order-one contact limit of the mixed-index (maximum, index-1 saddle) pair intensity after
fold normalization — is proven in the literature ONLY for isotropic fields (Section 2.3; sweep-5 verdict: no anisotropic d = 2 statement exists, published or preprint). Two natural repair
routes FAIL, and we record both failures before giving the proof that succeeds:
4.1 The coordinate-normalization route fails at fourth order (the Lambda_4
obstruction). A linear change of variables x -> A x can normalize the gradient covariance
Lambda_2 to the identity (the Cheng–Schwartzman-type normalization), after which the
field has isotropic SECOND-order structure. But stationary fields in d = 2 have fourth-order
spectral moment tensors Lambda_4 with more independent invariants than the two-parameter family GL(2)/O(2) of normalizations can absorb: writing the fourth-order
moments m_{jk} = integral k_1^j k_2^k rho(dk), j + k = 4, isotropy forces the Pearcey
relations (m_40 = m_04 = 3 m_22, m_31 = m_13 = 0 in normalized coordinates), FIVE
constraints on five moments of which a generic Lambda_2-normalized stationary field
satisfies none beyond the two that A can arrange. Since the mixed-index contact limit is a
functional of the joint jet law up to order >= 3, whose second-order block is Lambda_4, no
coordinate change reduces the anisotropic contact problem to the isotropic theorem.
[PROVEN-HERE at the level of the displayed invariant count; the count is elementary and

the sweep located the same obstruction discussed qualitatively in the anisotropy literature.]
4.2 The comparison/sandwich route fails structurally (Remark A6.4 below). Deferred to
its remark inside Section 5 so that the failure mode sits next to the correct proof.
5. The Isotropy-to-Anisotropy Bridge
5.1 Statement
Proposition A6 (anisotropic neutrality; theta-uniform order-one contact limit).
[PROVEN-HERE, MODULO exactly the same direction-independent finite-dimensional
positivity computation already carried by Proposition B2 (File 5, Section 4.1) — i.e., this
proposition ADDS NO new open obligation: it converts B2’s isotropic citation-plus-computation structure into a stationary frame-plus-computation structure with the SAME
residual computation.]
Let f satisfy (H1+)-(H2’) on T_L^2 (general stationary; no isotropy). For each direction theta
in S^1, let p_0(b, b - ell, r, theta) be the per-direction fold-pair density of File 5, Definition
3.1, and let k_2(r; b, theta) be its convergent-frame factor in the corrected divided-difference frame (File 3, Prop. 4.3; File 4, (3.3)-(3.4)). Then:
(i) (Order-one contact limit, per direction.) k_2(r; b, theta) -> k_2(0; b, theta) in [0, infinity)
as r -> 0, for every theta, uniformly for b in compacts; and k_2(0; b, theta) < infinity ALWAYS
(no divergence channel). (ii) (Theta-uniformity.) The convergence in (i) is uniform in theta in
S^1, and theta -> k_2(0; b, theta) is continuous. (iii) (Positivity.) k_2(0; b, theta) > 0 for
every theta iff the finite-dimensional limiting Gaussian functional charging the fold event is
positive — the SAME positivity statement as Proposition B2, now with theta as a compact
parameter; granted it (B2’s Phase-2 obligation, per direction, with continuity in theta
reducing the check to nondegeneracy plus a single open-condition verification), min over
theta of k_2(0; b, theta) > 0 and the theta-AVERAGED contact intensity of File 5, Section
3.1’s convention is order-one: 0 < c(B) <= liminf/limsup_{r -> 0} average_theta k_2(r; b,
theta) <= C(B) < infinity. (iv) (Consequence for the manuscript.) Every use of “neutrality” in
Files 1 and 5 (Prop. B2’s role in Theorem B; the change of variables of File 5 Section 5) is
valid verbatim for general stationary fields, with the constants rho_0(b), E_b[kappa^{-2/3}]
of File 5 (1.3) replaced by their theta-averaged forms — the exponent -1/3 is theta-blind, the
constant C_* acquires the angular average, exactly as File 1’s stress-table expectation
predicted (“anisotropy shifts constants, never exponents”).
5.2 Proof
The proof is a systematic audit of the frame machinery of Files 3-4 against the isotropy

hypothesis, converting “the literature proves this for isotropic fields” into “our frame proves
this for stationary fields, and isotropy was never used.” Each step names the statement it
leans on and the reason isotropy is absent from its proof.
STEP 1 (the frame and its limit are stationary objects). The corrected divided-difference
frame Psi_r^corr (File 4, (3.3)-(3.4)) is defined by finite linear combinations of jets at -+
(r/2) e_theta; its covariance entries are derivatives of the covariance kernel C at 0 and r
e_theta. Lemma P1 (File 4) proves Sigma(r, theta) -> Sigma(0, theta) entrywise with the limit
the covariance of six derivative functionals AT A POINT in the (t, s)-frame of direction theta.
Inputs to Lemma P1’s proof: Taylor expansion of C with Lambda_8-controlled remainders,
i.e. (H1+); nothing else. Isotropy status: never invoked; the limit Sigma(0, theta) simply
DEPENDS on theta through the directional derivatives — dependence is not obstruction.
STEP 2 (nondegeneracy of the limit frame is Lemma H(b), hence (H2’)-only). Sigma(0,
theta) is the Gram matrix of the six functionals ( f, f_t, f_s, f_tt, f_ts, f_ttt )(0) in the theta-rotated coordinates: pairwise-distinct derivative monomials. Lemma H(b) (File 4, Section
2.2) gives two-sided spectral bounds c_J <= Var(Q(D) f(0)) <= C_J on the unit coefficient
sphere from (H2’) alone — the polynomial-determinacy integral integral |Q(ik)|^2 rho(dk) is
a STATIONARY object; isotropy of rho was never asked. The rotation by theta acts on the
polynomial Q by composition with a rotation, a homeomorphism of the coefficient sphere:
the SAME constants c_J, C_J serve every theta. Hence spec(Sigma(0, theta)) subset [c, C]
with c, C theta-free. This is the single decisive point, and it is worth italicizing in referee
language: the isotropic literature proves neutrality by computing the contact limit in radial
coordinates; our architecture proves the nondegeneration of the contact FRAME from
spectral positivity, for which radial structure is irrelevant. The Lambda_4 obstruction of
Section 4.1 obstructs COORDINATE REDUCTION to the isotropic theorem; it does not
obstruct the frame proof, because the frame proof never leaves the anisotropic field.
STEP 3 (finiteness of the contact limit: (i)’s upper half). By File 3 Prop. 4.3 with File 4’s
corrected frame, k_2(r; b, theta) is the Gaussian density of the convergent frame at the
pinned values times the conditional expectation of the |det|-index-adjacency weights.
Convergence and finiteness: frame convergence (Step 1) + uniformly invertible limiting
Gramian (Step 2) + uniform weight moments (File 4, Theorem P2a(iii), whose proof used
Lemma P1 + regression calculus — again stationary). The Gaussian density at pinned values
is bounded by (2 pi)^{-3} (det restricted-block)^{-1/2} <= C by Step 2’s lower spectral
bound. No divergence channel exists: [0, infinity) in (i) can be sharpened to [0, C(B)] with
C(B) theta-free.
STEP 4 (theta-uniformity and continuity: (ii)). Sigma(r, theta) is jointly continuous in (r,
theta) on [0, r_0] x S^1 (entries are derivatives of C composed with rotations; continuity at r
= 0 by Step 1’s uniform Taylor remainders, which are theta-uniform because the remainder
bounds are norm bounds on Lambda_8-controlled tensors, rotation-invariant as BOUNDS

even though the tensors are not rotation-invariant as objects). A continuous matrix family
with spectra in a fixed [c, C] has continuous inverse and determinant; the weight
functionals’ conditional moments are continuous in the conditioning law by Gaussian
regression continuity (File 4, (2.1)) — composition gives joint continuity of k_2 on [0, r_0] x B
x S^1, and uniform convergence on the compact S^1 x B follows from continuity on a
compact product. This is the entire content of “uniformity by compactness of the circle”: no
estimate is redone; compactness converts pointwise limits of a continuous family into
uniform ones.
STEP 5 (positivity structure: (iii)). k_2(0; b, theta) is the limiting Gaussian functional: density
of the limit frame at the pinned fold values times the limiting weight expectation. Its
positivity is an OPEN-condition verification on a fixed finite-dimensional nondegenerate
Gaussian law — exactly Proposition B2’s designated Phase-2 computation, now
parametrized by theta. Two reductions keep the obligation from growing: (1) by Step 4,
theta -> k_2(0; b, theta) is continuous on compact S^1, so positivity for all theta follows
from no-zero, and a zero at some theta_0 would mean the limiting weight expectation
vanishes on a nondegenerate Gaussian law — possible only if the fold event { index
signature + adjacency } has probability zero under it, which is an open, checkable condition;
(2) for the theta-AVERAGED statement (iii) actually consumed by File 5’s convention
(Section 3.1 there), positivity of the AVERAGE requires positivity at a single theta. We
nevertheless state and will verify the per-theta form, because the averaged form’s
sufficiency should not tempt the program into leaving a possible exceptional-direction
phenomenon unexamined — if k_2(0; b, theta_0) = 0 occurred at isolated directions it would
be a REportable structural discovery, not an inconvenience. [Reduction PROVEN-HERE; the
positivity computation itself carries B2’s Phase-2 label, unchanged in difficulty: the isotropic
instance plus Step-4 continuity plus the open-condition argument covers a neighborhood of
every theta once verified at finitely many.]
STEP 6 (the independent upper cross-check). Muirhead 2020 (Section 2.2(b)) provides, for
generic STATIONARY planar fields, a second-moment/no-attraction bound for critical
points: the two-point critical intensity admits an integrable upper envelope at small
separation with no attraction singularity. Consistency check: our Step-3 finiteness must not
exceed what his bound permits after un-normalizing the frame factors — it does not: |det
T_2(r)|^{-1} times a bounded k_2 reproduces a two-point intensity within his envelope’s
order (the fold channel’s Theta(r^2) soft-determinant factors included, per File 3 Lemma
6.5). The cross-check is logged as verification V6.1: an INDEPENDENT stationary-hypothesis result bounding us from above, so that Proposition A6’s finiteness half is doubly
attested — once by our frame, once by the literature’s only stationary two-point statement.
What Muirhead 2020 does NOT provide — the order-one LOWER structure and the mixed-channel isolation — is exactly what Steps 1-5 supply. QED (at the labels displayed in 5.1).

5.3 What Proposition A6 changes in the manuscript’s ledger
Proposition B2’s label decomposes as: [frame structure and theta-uniformity: PROVEN-HERE (this file) + Files 3-4] + [finite-dimensional positivity: Phase-2 computation, per-theta with the Step-5 reductions]. The isotropic literature (Azaïs- Delmas; BCW) is RE-CLASSIFIED from “input” to “input for the isotropic instance + independent
corroboration of the mechanism”: the manuscript’s stationary claims no longer route any
load through an isotropic hypothesis. File 1’s Scope Remark 3.4 is to be annotated
accordingly (patch directive P6.1: the anisotropic sector is now “analytically closed
modulo the same Phase-2 positivity computation as the isotropic sector,” while
remaining numerically untested — the calibration gap stands).
No new open item is created; one open item (B2 positivity) gains a compact parameter
and a continuity reduction.
5.4 Remark A6.4 (the rejected route, on the record).
[PROVEN-HERE at the level of the displayed failure mode.] A natural- looking alternative
proof was considered and REJECTED before drafting: bound the anisotropic kernel between
isotropic majorant/ minorant kernels (“local ellipticity”) and sandwich the contact limit
between the two isotropic Azaïs–Delmas baselines, with an Euler-characteristic robustness
heuristic supplying the mixed-channel transfer. The route fails structurally, twice. First,
pointwise kernel domination does not yield monotone comparison of Kac-Rice pair
functionals: Slepian-type comparison theorems govern suprema and level-exceedance
probabilities, NOT conditional expectations of |det Hessian| weights, which enter the pair
intensity with both signs of dependence on covariance perturbations — there is no
comparison principle for k_2 in the kernel order, and any sandwich assembled from one
would be unlicensed at its first inequality. Second, the Euler-characteristic heuristic controls
the INDEX BALANCE (alternating sums across channels), not the size of any one channel:
chi-based robustness is compatible with the mixed-channel intensity degenerating while
extremal channels compensate, so it cannot certify an order-one limit. The route is filed as a
refuted candidate (adjacent to, but not entered in, the kill registry — like File 5’s r^4 item, it
was caught at the design stage and never became a program claim). Its documentation here
is deliberate referee-facing practice: the reviewer who thinks of the sandwich should find, in
the manuscript, the reason it does not work.
6. Smoothness reconciliation: the final ledger
6.1 What C^3-class regularity buys, and the re-anchored citation
For the TOPOLOGICAL and counting layer — a.s. Morse structure, distinct critical values,

finiteness of critical-point moments, the well-definedness of the persistence diagram and of
the elder pairing — C^3 sample regularity with the corresponding spectral-moment
nondegeneracies suffices. Verified anchors: Azaïs–Wschebor 2009 (Kac-Rice validity layer,
Section 2.1) and Gass–Stecconi 2024 (PTRF 190; arXiv:2305.17586) for critical-point
moment finiteness under minimal smoothness (Section 2.6). AUDIT NOTE (citation hygiene,
on the record): an earlier candidate anchor for the C^3-sufficiency sentence — a Hirsch–
Lachièze-Rey item carried in a working note as arXiv:2411.11429 — was checked in sweep 5
and found to be a different object (a functional-CLT-type result for persistent Betti numbers,
not a minimal-smoothness sufficiency statement for the critical-point layer); it is therefore
NOT cited for this purpose anywhere in the manuscript, and the sufficiency sentence rests
on the two verified anchors above plus our own File 2. [Boundary map PROVEN-HERE;
records verified, sweep 5.]
6.2 Why our architecture needs more, exactly where, and exactly
how much
The manuscript’s quantitative spine requires, beyond the C^3 layer:
(a) Lambda_8 < infinity — equivalently the C^{4}-class L^2-jet condition written into (H1+)
— consumed at PRECISELY TWO places: (i) File 4, Theorem P2(b)’s UPPER bounds: the
Theta(tau^4) residual scaling on the axis (the tau^8-variance row), whose proof exhibits the
two-point Hermite competitor and sums the interpolation-error symbol |k|^4 tau^4 against
rho — summability IS Lambda_8; and (ii) File 4, Lemma P1’s displayed convergence-rate
bookkeeping for the corrected frame (with the minimal-modulus question logged as O4.2,
likely relaxable, not pursued). Downstream consumers of (i): every exp(-c/tau^2)
suppression in the manuscript — File 3’s Lemma A’ route, the band Lemma B1, Lemma I’s
localization (Prop. 7.1 there) — i.e. the entire mechanism that DELETED the two-parameter
(K, r) architecture (kill-registry K2). The lower bounds of P2(b) and all of Lemma H need
only (H2’). (b) (H1++) — the eighth-order modulus refinement — consumed ONLY by File 3’s
inner layer (Lemma 6.1’s top-order W_0-covariance limits), with the explicit relaxation trade
recorded there (File 3, Remark 6.2: shrink the inner radius to r^{2 - epsilon} and (H1+)
suffices at an epsilon-degraded beta). Since Lemma I is in any case conditional on (ND), the
marginal hypothesis cost of (H1++) is confined to the manuscript’s single conditional
chapter. (c) The general-nu degradation (File 4, Proposition P5): when Lambda_8 = infinity
but the spectral tail has effective smoothness nu in (3, 4), the tau^4 scaling degrades to
tau^{nu + 1/2} and every suppression survives super-polynomially — so Theorems A-B are
ROBUST in mechanism down to the C^3 boundary, with constants degrading as nu
decreases; the manuscript’s sharp-rate statements, not its limits, are what Lambda_8 buys.
This is the reconciliation sentence the referee should take away: C^3 is where the OBJECTS
live; Lambda_8 < infinity is where our RATES live; and the gap between them is populated by
Proposition P5’s continuum of intermediate statements, matching (File 1, (H1+) note) the

kernel-ordered finite-scale corrections observed in the program’s calibration archive.
